query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under service conditions, the creep resistance of a protective FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy coating is enhanced by the in situ, stress‐activated formation of nano‐sized precipitates along the coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries. These dynamically formed precipitates act as robust barriers to dislocation climb and glide, raising the effective activation energy for creep and thereby markedly slowing the accumulation of plastic strain.
generation.material_initial_state: A protective coating composed of an FCC/BCC dual-phase high-entropy alloy with clean, coherent interphase boundaries and a uniform microstructure (i.e. minimal pre-existing nano‐precipitates).
generation.intervention: Subject the coating to sustained, continuous mechanical loading at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 500–600°C) that is sufficient to activate lattice diffusion. At the same time, conduct a controlled comparison by processing a variant of the coating to suppress dynamic precipitate formation (for example, via a rapid quench after deposition or altered heat-treatment parameters).
generation.conditions: Intermediate temperatures and stresses where dislocation climb is active but below the regime where catastrophic recrystallization or phase transformation dominates. The comparison should be made under identical loading conditions to isolate the effect of dynamic interphase precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: The dynamic formation of nano‐precipitates— and the associated possible development of undulated or serrated FCC/BCC boundaries— which serve as strong barriers to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained loading at elevated temperature, stress-assisted lattice diffusion enables dislocations to climb; however, as deformation progresses, localized compositional fluctuations and dynamic recrystallization promote the nucleation and growth of nano‐precipitates along the FCC/BCC interfaces. These precipitates increase the local obstacle stress needed for dislocation motion, thereby both increasing the stress exponent and the apparent activation energy for creep. In the processed coating variant designed to enhance precipitate formation, these effects collectively slow the evolution of creep strain compared to a coating where such features are absent.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coating variant that develops dynamic interphase nano‐precipitates will exhibit a significantly lower steady-state creep strain rate, a higher stress exponent, and extended creep rupture life under identical testing compared to the control coating lacking such precipitates. Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM) should reveal an increased density of nano‐precipitates along the FCC/BCC interfaces in the improved sample.
generation.baseline: The starting microstructure is the as-deposited dual-phase FCC/BCC coating with smooth, unmodified interfaces and minimal pre-existing precipitate features.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective in the intermediate temperature window (~500–600°C) and under continuous loading where diffusion‐assisted dislocation climb is active. At significantly higher temperatures or stresses that trigger alternative deformation modes (such as extensive phase transformation), the barrier effect of dynamically formed precipitates may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: While earlier work on FCC high-entropy alloys (PMC7512559, section '5_conclusions' and related discussion) and on the influence of lattice misfit (PMC12842692, section '3_4_effect_of_lattice_misfit_on_the_cree') supports the concept of interfacial obstacles enhancing creep resistance, the precise quantitative impact of dynamically formed nano-precipitates along FCC/BCC boundaries in a dual-phase protective coating remains uncertain and requires targeted experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy coatings: one processed to promote dynamic nano-precipitate formation along the interphase boundaries (e.g., by applying a controlled heat-treatment and sustaining a moderate load at 500–600°C) and a second set processed to inhibit such precipitation (e.g., via rapid quenching post-deposition). Subject both sets to identical continuous loading conditions at the selected temperature and monitor creep behavior over time.
measurements: Steady-state creep strain rate as determined from strain-time curves
Stress exponent and apparent activation energy extracted through log–log analysis of strain rate versus applied stress
Microstructural imaging (e.g., TEM) to quantify the presence and distribution of nano-precipitates along FCC/BCC interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating engineered to promote dynamic precipitate formation does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate (or equivalently, does not show an increased stress exponent/activation energy) compared to the coating in which such precipitates are suppressed, then the hypothesis that dynamic interphase nano-precipitates enhance creep resistance is falsified.

This transformation is driven by the misfit-induced strain energy, with δ serving as a key indicator of morphological stability. In general, a cubic morphology minimizes the alloy’s strain energy and enhances precipitate stability. However, when the value of |δ| becomes excessively large, the interfacial stress rises sharply, destabilizing the phase morphology and degrading creep resistance. This accounts for the observed non-monotonic relationship between |δ| and creep life. The intermediate-temperature creep behavior and microstructural evolution of CoCrFeNiMn HEA have been studied. Optical micrographs and TEM images of the dislocation substructure after creep deformation revealed the effects of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation on the deformation mechanisms. The following conclusions can be drawn:An obvious transition in stress exponent and average activation energy was observed: At low stresses, the values were approximately 5 to 6 and 268 kJ/mol, whereas at high-stress regions, the corresponding values were 8.9–14 and 380 kJ/mol. Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion is suggested as a possible rate-dominating mechanism at low stresses.At high stresses, obvious dynamic recrystallization occurred, leading to the refinement of average grain size. Simultaneously, nano-sized M23C6 carbides and the Cr-rich tetragonal σ phase were dynamically precipitated. High density of tangled and curved dislocation substructures was observed.
